title: Will a Hangover Cause a Fever? Chills, Flu, or Something Else
excerpt: Feeling hot and shivery after drinking? Why hangovers feel feverish, why a real temperature usually means infection, how to tell a hangover from the flu, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can a hangover cause a fever? Why you feel hot and shivery after drinking, what a real temperature means, safe fever medicine, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a normal hangover can make you feel hot, shivery, achy, and generally "flu-ish," but it doesn't usually cause a true fever. If a thermometer reads **100.4°F (38°C) or higher**, the most likely explanation is that something else is going on, most often an infection you picked up around the same time you were drinking. Alcohol itself tends to *lower* your core body temperature, not raise it. So the feeling of being feverish is common after a big night, while a measured fever is a signal to look for another cause.

This guide explains why hangovers make you feel feverish, how to tell a hangover from the flu, COVID, or food poisoning, what a real temperature after drinking can mean, how to treat it safely (some fever medicines don't mix well with alcohol), and when to get medical help.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get medical care promptly if** your temperature is 103°F (39.4°C) or higher, a fever lasts more than two days, or you have a fever along with a stiff neck, a bad headache that won't ease, confusion, a new rash, trouble breathing or chest pain, severe belly pain (especially pain that spreads to your back), yellow skin or eyes, or you can't keep fluids down. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if someone is very hot and confused after drinking or using other drugs, is hard to wake, is having a seizure, or is breathing slowly or irregularly. If you drink heavily most days and develop shaking, sweating, a racing heart, and a raised temperature a day or two after stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal. It can become dangerous, so get medical help rather than waiting it out.

## Will a Hangover Cause a Fever?

Usually, no. The standard list of hangover symptoms that researchers use includes headache, tiredness, thirst, nausea, sensitivity to light and sound, poor sleep, trouble concentrating, and a general sense of feeling unwell. Sweating and shivering show up on some symptom scales too. A true fever, meaning a measured rise in core body temperature, is not one of the core features. (For the full list, see our guide to [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms).)

What *is* common is the feeling of being feverish. People describe it as:

- Feeling hot and flushed one minute and cold the next
- Chills or shivering while lying in bed
- Clammy skin or night sweats
- Aches in the muscles and joints
- That heavy, wiped-out feeling you get with a virus

All of this can happen with a perfectly normal body temperature. If you take your temperature and it reads 98 or 99°F (about 37°C), you're most likely dealing with a hangover. If it reads 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, which is the threshold the CDC and most doctors use to define a fever, treat that as a clue that something besides the alcohol is involved.

### A low-grade temperature is a gray zone

A reading in the 99.5 to 100.3°F range (about 37.5 to 37.9°C) is harder to interpret. Body temperature naturally varies through the day, it's often slightly higher in the late afternoon, and a hot shower, a warm room, heavy blankets, or a hot drink can all nudge a reading up. Dehydration may raise it a little too. A slightly warm reading the morning after drinking, with no other new symptoms, isn't usually a cause for alarm. Re-check it in a few hours after you've had water and rested. If it climbs or stays up, take that seriously.

## Why a Hangover Makes You Feel Feverish

There are several real, well-understood reasons a hangover can mimic the feel of being sick, even without an actual fever.

### 1. Your immune system is stirred up

Researchers have measured immune signaling molecules called **cytokines** in people with hangovers. These are the same chemical messengers your body releases when you're fighting an infection, and they're a big part of why being sick makes you feel achy, tired, and foggy. Studies of hangovers have found changes in several cytokines after a night of heavy drinking, and some found that higher levels lined up with worse hangover symptoms. The research is still fairly small, but the idea that hangovers involve an inflammatory response is widely accepted among hangover researchers.

That helps explain why a hangover can feel so much like coming down with something. Your body is running a milder version of the same "I'm sick" program, which brings fatigue, aches, and that general feverish malaise. It doesn't usually push your temperature into fever range the way a real infection does.

### 2. Alcohol scrambles your temperature control

Alcohol widens the blood vessels near your skin (doctors call this vasodilation). That's why you feel warm and flushed while drinking. But the warm feeling is misleading. More blood near the skin means you lose heat faster, so your core temperature tends to **drop** while you're drinking. This is the reason people who pass out drunk in the cold are at real risk of hypothermia, and why the old idea of a "warming" shot of brandy is a myth.

As the alcohol wears off, your body works to bring its temperature back to normal. Swings between feeling hot and feeling cold, sweating, then shivering, are part of that readjustment. They can feel very much like the chills of a fever.

### 3. Night sweats and a wet bed

Many people wake up drenched after drinking. Alcohol can raise your heart rate, open up blood vessels, and disturb the brain's temperature control, all of which can trigger sweating. Then you lie there in damp sheets and get cold. Wake up shivering in a sweat-soaked T-shirt and it's easy to assume you have a fever. Our guide to [night sweats after drinking](/never-hungover/night-sweats-after-drinking) covers this in more detail.

### 4. Dehydration and low blood sugar

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink, and a night of drinking often comes with sweating and sometimes vomiting. Being low on fluids can leave you feeling weak, lightheaded, and achy. Alcohol can also lower blood sugar, especially if you didn't eat much, which can cause shakiness, sweating, and clamminess. None of these is a fever, but together they produce a lot of the same sensations.

### 5. Poor sleep

Alcohol may knock you out quickly, but it fragments the second half of the night. You get less deep, restful sleep and wake up more often. Sleep loss on its own makes people feel run down and achy, and it's tied to the same inflammatory signals mentioned above. A short, broken night stacks on top of everything else.

### 6. Shakes and a racing heart

Trembling hands and a pounding heart are common the morning after, especially after heavy drinking. They come from your nervous system rebounding as the alcohol leaves. Shaking can feel like shivering from a fever, but it's a different thing. See our guides on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) and [body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking) for more on those symptoms.

## Hangover Chills: Why You Feel Cold After Drinking

"Hangover chills" is one of the most common ways people describe this. Here's what's usually behind them:

- **Heat loss from the night before.** If you spent the evening flushed and warm, you lost heat through your skin. Walking home in cold weather or falling asleep without covers makes it worse.
- **Wet skin from sweating.** Sweat evaporating off your skin cools you down, sometimes enough to set off shivering.
- **Low blood sugar.** Not eating much plus alcohol can drop your blood sugar and leave you cold and shaky.
- **Your body's thermostat resetting.** As described above, temperature control is a bit off for a while after drinking.

Chills that come with a normal temperature and fade as you eat, drink fluids, and warm up are typical of a hangover. Chills that come with a real fever, keep coming back in waves, or bring on violent, teeth-chattering shaking point more toward an infection.

## Is It a Hangover or Am I Getting Sick?

This is the real question behind most searches for "hangover fever." Parties, bars, festivals, and crowded flights are good places to catch something, and a few days of late nights, little sleep, and drinking don't do your defenses any favors. So it's entirely possible to have a hangover and a cold or flu at the same time. A few clues help separate them.

**Signs it's probably just a hangover:**

- Your temperature is normal, or only slightly warm and coming down
- Symptoms are worst in the morning and steadily improve through the day
- You feel noticeably better after water, food, and rest
- No cough, sore throat, runny nose, or loss of taste or smell
- You're mostly back to normal within about 24 hours

**Signs it's probably something else:**

- A measured temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or more
- Symptoms are getting *worse* as the day goes on instead of better
- A sore throat, cough, congestion, or sneezing
- Body aches that feel deeper and heavier than your usual hangover
- New loss of taste or smell
- You still feel just as bad (or worse) the next day

A useful rule: **hangovers get better, infections often get worse.** Most hangovers peak in the morning and clear within a day. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains the usual timeline. If your symptoms are heading in the opposite direction, assume you're sick.

### Hangover vs. flu

The flu tends to start suddenly with a fever, chills, deep muscle aches, headache, and exhaustion, often with a dry cough and sore throat. That overlaps a lot with a rough hangover, which is why people mix them up. The giveaways are the thermometer and the trajectory: flu usually brings a genuine fever and gets worse over the first couple of days rather than improving by the afternoon.

### Hangover vs. COVID

COVID can look like a cold, the flu, or very little at all. Fever, cough, sore throat, congestion, fatigue, and loss of taste or smell are all possible. If you were in a crowd and now have a fever or cold symptoms, a home test is a quick way to check. A normal hangover won't make a COVID test positive.

### Hangover vs. food poisoning

Late-night food, buffet dishes left out too long, and undercooked takeaway are classic culprits. Food poisoning usually brings vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach cramps, and some types cause a fever. A hangover can also upset your stomach, but repeated diarrhea, cramping, and a fever point more toward a bug. Keep up with fluids, and get medical help if you see blood in your stool, can't keep fluids down, or show signs of dehydration such as very little urine or dizziness when you stand. If diarrhea is your main symptom, our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) covers the alcohol-related causes.

## What a Real Fever After Drinking Can Mean

If you've confirmed a genuine fever, here are the main possibilities, roughly from most to least common for an otherwise healthy social drinker.

### An ordinary infection

By far the most likely. Colds, flu, COVID, strep throat, and stomach bugs are all easy to catch on a night out. Shared drinks, close conversations, and crowded rooms make it easier still. Treat it like any other infection: rest, fluids, and see a doctor if it's severe or lasts.

### Aspiration after vomiting

If someone vomited while very drunk, especially while lying down or half-asleep, there's a risk of breathing some of it into the lungs. This can lead to a lung infection or inflammation, sometimes called aspiration pneumonia. Warning signs over the next day or two include fever, a cough (sometimes with discolored mucus), chest pain, and shortness of breath. This needs medical attention, so don't write it off as a lingering hangover.

### Heat illness

A long day drinking in the sun at a festival, beach, or barbecue can cause heat exhaustion, and in serious cases heat stroke. Alcohol makes this more likely because it adds to fluid loss and dulls your sense that you're overheating. Heat stroke, with a very high temperature, confusion, and hot skin, is a medical emergency. Call 911.

### Mixing alcohol with other drugs

Stimulant drugs such as MDMA ("molly"), cocaine, and amphetamines can drive body temperature dangerously high, particularly in hot, crowded spaces with dancing. A very hot, confused, agitated person after a night of drinking and drug use needs emergency care right away. Some medicine combinations can also cause raised temperature with agitation, sweating, and muscle twitching. If you're on prescription medicine, especially an antidepressant, and you develop those symptoms after a night out, get medical help.

### Pancreatitis

Heavy drinking, and sometimes a single large binge, can inflame the pancreas. The hallmark is severe pain in the upper belly that often spreads to the back, usually with nausea and vomiting, and sometimes a fever. This is not a hangover and needs urgent medical care.

### Alcohol withdrawal

This one applies to people who drink heavily most days, not to someone who had a big Saturday. When a person whose body is used to daily alcohol suddenly stops or cuts back sharply, withdrawal can start within hours to a couple of days. Signs include shaking, sweating, anxiety, a racing heart, trouble sleeping, and sometimes a raised temperature. In its severe form it can cause confusion, hallucinations, seizures, and high fever, and it can be life-threatening. If this sounds like you or someone you're with, it's a medical problem that doctors treat every day. Contact a doctor or go to an urgent care or emergency department, and don't try to tough it out alone.

### Liver inflammation in heavy drinkers

In people who have been drinking heavily for a long time, alcohol-related hepatitis can cause fever along with yellowing of the skin or eyes, belly pain or swelling, and feeling very unwell. It's uncommon in occasional drinkers, but yellow skin or eyes after drinking is always a reason to see a doctor promptly.

## How to Take Your Temperature Accurately After Drinking

Since the thermometer is the deciding factor, it's worth getting a reliable reading:

1. **Wait 20 to 30 minutes after eating, drinking, or brushing your teeth** before taking an oral temperature. A hot coffee or cold water will throw off the reading.
2. **Wait after a hot shower** or after getting out from under heavy covers, since both can make you read warm.
3. **Use the same method each time.** Oral, ear, and forehead thermometers give slightly different numbers. Stick with one so you can see the trend.
4. **Check more than once.** A single borderline reading means little. A pattern over several hours tells you much more.
5. **Write down the numbers and times.** If you end up calling a doctor, this is exactly what they'll want to know.

## How to Feel Better (and Bring Down a Real Fever) Safely

### If it's a hangover with a normal temperature

- **Drink water steadily** through the morning. An electrolyte drink can help if you were sweating or vomiting. Our comparison of [electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) covers the options.
- **Eat something easy,** like toast, crackers, bananas, rice, or eggs, to bring your blood sugar back up.
- **Change into dry clothes and sheets** if you sweated through them, then warm up with a blanket.
- **Rest.** Sleep is the one thing that reliably helps the achy, run-down feeling.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** More alcohol only delays the crash and adds to the strain on your body.

### Fever medicine after drinking: choose carefully

The two common fever reducers each have a catch when alcohol is involved.

**Acetaminophen (Tylenol, also called paracetamol)** is easy on the stomach, but your liver processes both it and alcohol, and the combination can be hard on the liver, especially at high doses or in people who drink heavily on a regular basis. The FDA label tells anyone who has 3 or more drinks every day to ask a doctor before using it. Many cold and flu products also contain acetaminophen, so it's easy to double up by accident. If you use it, take a single standard dose once the alcohol has cleared, eat first, and stay well under the daily limit. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the risks in detail.

**Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) and naproxen (Aleve)** are easier on the liver but harder on the stomach and kidneys. Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining, and these medicines carry a label warning about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. If you choose one, take it with food and water and stick to the label dose. If you're dehydrated, ibuprofen also adds strain to the kidneys, so rehydrate first. See our guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol), or our side-by-side look at [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover).

**Read the label on combination cold and flu products.** "Nighttime" and multi-symptom formulas often combine acetaminophen with antihistamines or other ingredients that cause drowsiness, which stacks with any alcohol still in your system. If you're not sure what's in a product, ask a pharmacist.

**When in doubt, ask a pharmacist.** They can look at your full list of medicines and tell you what's safest for you. That's especially worth doing if you take prescription medicine, have liver or kidney problems, or have stomach ulcers.

### If you're actually sick

Treat the infection, not the hangover. Stay home, rest, drink plenty of fluids, and avoid alcohol until you've recovered. Alcohol can interfere with your immune response and with sleep, both of which you need to get better. Our article on [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) covers this, and [does alcohol help a cold?](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-help-a-cold) tackles the hot-toddy myth. If you're prescribed antibiotics or antiviral medicine, check with your pharmacist about alcohol, since some medicines interact with it badly.

## Can Drinking While Sick Make a Fever Worse?

It can make you feel worse and slow your recovery, even though alcohol doesn't directly cause a fever. Drinking while you're fighting an infection adds dehydration on top of a fever that's already costing you fluids, worsens sleep at the time your body needs it most, and may blunt parts of your immune response. It also complicates which fever medicines you can safely take. If you already have a fever, the sensible move is to hold off on drinking until you're well.

## Why Some People Feel Feverish After Even a Few Drinks

If you regularly feel hot, flushed, and unwell after a small amount of alcohol, a few explanations are worth knowing:

- **Alcohol flush reaction.** Many people, particularly of East Asian descent, carry a gene variant that slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. The result is facial redness, warmth, a fast heartbeat, and nausea after just a drink or two. It's a sign of acetaldehyde building up, and it's linked to a higher risk of certain cancers with regular drinking. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) goes deeper.
- **Histamine and sulfite sensitivity.** Some people react to histamine in red wine and certain beers, which can cause flushing, warmth, a stuffy nose, and headache.
- **Medication interactions.** Several medicines, including metronidazole and some others, can cause a strong reaction with alcohol that includes flushing and a hot, unwell feeling. If you're on a new prescription and react badly to a drink, check with your pharmacist.
- **Age.** Many people find hangovers hit harder as they get older. Our article on [why hangovers get worse with age](/never-hungover/why-hangovers-get-worse-with-age) explains some of the likely reasons.

If you get a genuine fever every time you drink, even a small amount, that isn't normal. Talk to a doctor about it.

## Reducing the Odds of a Feverish, Flu-Like Hangover

The best way to avoid waking up shivery and sore is to keep the hangover itself smaller. The habits with the best support are simple:

- **Drink less and drink slower.** The amount you drink is the strongest predictor of how bad the next morning is.
- **Alternate alcoholic drinks with water.** This slows your pace and limits dehydration.
- **Eat a real meal before and while drinking.** Food slows the rate alcohol reaches your blood and helps steady blood sugar.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can, and give yourself time to sleep it off.
- **Dress for the walk home.** Alcohol makes you feel warmer than you are, so bring a layer in cold weather.
- **Don't share drinks during cold and flu season.** It's an easy way to pass infections around.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through these in more detail.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents fevers, treats infections, or protects you from any of the more serious causes covered above, and it doesn't make it safe to drink while you're sick. If you want to try it as part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Will a hangover cause a fever?**

Usually not. A hangover commonly makes you feel hot, shivery, sweaty, and achy, but a measured temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher isn't a typical hangover symptom. Alcohol actually tends to lower core body temperature. If you have a real fever after drinking, the most likely cause is an infection you picked up around the same time.

**Why do I feel feverish and have chills after drinking?**

Several things combine: a mild inflammatory response from your immune system, alcohol widening the blood vessels in your skin (which makes you lose heat), night sweats that leave you damp and cold, dehydration, low blood sugar, and poor sleep. Together they can feel very much like a fever even when your temperature is normal.

**Can a hangover cause a low-grade fever?**

A slightly warm reading, around 99.5 to 100.3°F (37.5 to 37.9°C), can come from normal daily variation, a warm room, a hot drink, or dehydration. If it settles after you drink water and rest, it was probably nothing. If it climbs to 100.4°F or higher or stays up, look for another cause such as an infection.

**How can I tell if it's a hangover or the flu?**

Use a thermometer and watch the direction of your symptoms. Hangovers usually peak in the morning and steadily improve through the day, with a normal temperature and no cough or sore throat. The flu typically brings a real fever, deep body aches, and often a cough or sore throat, and tends to get worse over the first day or two rather than better.

**Can I take Tylenol for a fever after drinking?**

For most healthy adults who don't drink heavily day to day, a single standard dose once the alcohol has cleared and after eating is unlikely to cause harm. Stay well under the daily limit and check other cold and flu products for hidden acetaminophen. If you have 3 or more drinks most days or have liver problems, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

**Is ibuprofen better than Tylenol for a fever after drinking?**

Neither is risk-free. Ibuprofen is easier on the liver but harder on the stomach and kidneys, and alcohol already irritates the stomach. Take it with food and water, rehydrate first, and stick to the label dose. A pharmacist can help you choose based on your health and other medicines.

**When should I see a doctor for a fever after drinking?**

Get care if your temperature is 103°F (39.4°C) or higher, a fever lasts more than two days, or it comes with a stiff neck, confusion, a rash, trouble breathing, chest pain, severe belly pain, yellow skin or eyes, or an inability to keep fluids down. Call 911 for someone who is very hot and confused, hard to wake, having a seizure, or breathing slowly. If you drink heavily most days and develop shaking, sweating, and a raised temperature after stopping, get medical help, since that can be alcohol withdrawal.

**Can drinking while sick make a fever worse?**

Alcohol doesn't directly cause a fever, but drinking while you're fighting an infection adds dehydration, disrupts the sleep you need to recover, and may weaken parts of your immune response. It also limits which fever medicines are safe to take. It's best to skip alcohol until you're better.
